findings.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential persists the generated recovery codes as a raw plaintext JSON list (recoveryCodesJson written as challengeResponse / credentialData) whenever the user storage accepts the credential, with no hashing applied. Any real user-storage provider that supports the recovery-codes type receives the raw codes via input.getChallengeResponse() and stores them unhashed (the diff's own test provider persists JsonSerialization of the raw list as credentialData), so plaintext one-time secrets sit at rest in external storages, unlike the local path where credentialModel stores only hashed codes and salt.

[BUG] The user-storage branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential provides no mechanism to mark an individual code as used, because the one-shot UserCredentialModel.updateCredential call only ever writes the full raw list on (re)generation. For user-storage users every recovery code remains valid forever (the storage provider's isValid in this diff compares the submitted code against the full original list with no consumed-code tracking), so a leaked code can be replayed indefinitely, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean always prompts for code number 0 since the rebuilt model from createFromValues never has any code marked used.

[ADVISORY] The recovery-codes credential provider is looked up via the hardcoded string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, which the removed code in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction previously used. The provider id is now maintained in two places (the factory constant and this literal); if the constant is ever changed or a deployer swaps the provider, the literal silently resolves to null and createCredential throws an NPE at recovery-code setup time for local-storage users.

[ADVISORY] configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes registers a "delayed-authenticator" execution with a delay config (and a misspelled alias "delayed-suthenticator-config") even though every caller in this diff passes delay=0, making the delayed subflow dead weight that must resolve successfully for the test to run. If the "delayed-authenticator" provider id does not exist in the test auth-server's deployed providers, FlowUtil.addAuthenticatorExecution fails and testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin errors before reaching any assertion; even when it resolves, the next maintainer must edit this flow wiring to change any test's timing behavior.

[ADVISORY] getCredential's javadoc claims it checks "the user storage" then local storage, but getFederatedCredentialsStream on SubjectCredentialManager returns credentials exposed via the storage provider's getCredentials, which for providers that do not implement that lookup (or that fail JSON deserialization as in the diff's own BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials IOException path) silently yields an empty stream that falls through to local storage with no error. A user whose recovery codes exist in a storage whose getCredentials hits the deserialization error branch (logged at error, credential omitted) will fall through to the local-storage lookup, find nothing, and the caller RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then throws NoSuchElementException on credentialModelOpt.get(), producing a 500 on the login form instead of a credential-missing challenge.

[BUG] Federated recovery codes are validated with raw string equality and never consumed or invalidated, so a recovery code stored in user storage is reusable an unlimited number of times. Recovery authn codes are a one-time-use credential by contract (the local keycloak-recovery-authn-codes provider removes each used code); a user whose codes live in user storage can replay the same leaked code indefinitely, and the test testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin verifies a single successful login without ever attempting reuse, so this silent drop of the single-use acceptance criterion ships undetected.

[BUG] The local-storage fallback branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential (the else path when userStorageCreated is false) is exercised by no test in the diff. The diff's only new test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) uses a storage that returns true from updateCredential, so the entire reason this helper exists — a user storage that does not support recovery codes falling back to the Keycloak DB provider — is unverified; a regression in the fallback (e.g. wrong provider id 'keycloak-recovery-authn-codes' or a null provider crash) would leave users unable to set up recovery codes at all and no test would fail.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential ships the raw, unhashed recovery codes as a JSON string in the UserCredentialModel challengeResponse, establishing a cleartext transport/storage contract for any user-storage implementation, in contrast to the local provider path which stores only hashed codes. Any third-party user-storage provider adopting this contract will persist recovery codes in plaintext, and a leak of that external store yields directly usable credentials; operators enabling recovery codes on federated realms get a materially weaker security posture than on local realms with no warning or documentation of this difference in the diff.

[ADVISORY] RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls credentialModelOpt.get() without checking presence, so a user who reaches the recovery-code login page with no credential in either federated or local storage throws NoSuchElementException during bean construction. The previous code had the same findFirst().get() crash, but this diff broadened the lookup to include federated credentials — a new failure surface (a storage whose getFederatedCredentialsStream returns an empty stream for a user the authenticator just accepted) now triggers an unhandled 500 on the login page render; the refactor was the opportunity to make this render a proper error and it was not taken.

[ADVISORY] getCredential gives federated credentials unconditional precedence over local ones, and there is no test covering the case where both a stale local recovery-codes credential and a fresh federated one exist. When a user migrates or a realm toggles storage support, a user with an old local recovery-codes credential plus a new federated one will silently authenticate against the federated set, and code numbering shown on the login page (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean uses the same lookup) can disagree with the codes the user actually holds; the shadowing precedence is a behavior decision with zero verification in the diff.

[ADVISORY] This PR modifies BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, whose declared contract is that the provider is source-frozen at Keycloak 4.8.3 so future Keycloak versions can be tested against an unmodified legacy provider. The class comment still says 'Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider', but this diff changes its source (adds recovery-code handling, getCredentials override, generated ids), so the backwards-compatibility guarantee the test exists to verify is no longer exercised — a future regression against legacy user storages ships undetected because the reference legacy provider now uses new APIs (KeycloakModelUtils.generateId, getCredentials stream contract).

[ADVISORY] configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes injects a 'delayed-authenticator' execution with a configurable delay parameter that has no connection to this PR's stated intent (recovery key support for user storage providers). The test wires an extra 'delayed-authenticator' execution (with a 'delayed-suthenticator-config' alias typo) and a delay parameter that the single caller passes as 0; this is copied machinery from the recovery-codes form test and inflates the user-storage test with flow configuration the scenario never exercises — the next maintainer of browser-flow tests must reason about why a user-storage test owns a delay knob that is always 0.

[ADVISORY] The refactor to RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns Optional, but the caller immediately calls .get() unconditionally, so the Optional wrapping enforces nothing and the empty case still throws NoSuchElementException. A user who reaches the recovery-code login form without a recovery credential of either kind (e.g. credential deleted between flow setup and form render) gets a raw NoSuchElementException / 500 from the login form instead of a graceful error; the refactor moved the lookup but left the failure semantics untouched, which is dead structure that signals safety that does not exist.

[ADVISORY] The federated-storage fallback is only wired into the required-action path (RecoveryAuthnCodesAction), leaving the other credential-creation path — the account console / admin REST createCredential for recovery codes — still calling the local provider directly, so the 'recovery keys in user storage' invariant is not enforced across all creation entry points. A federated user who sets up recovery codes through the account console (or admin REST) gets the credential written to the local Keycloak DB instead of their user storage, producing a split-brain: the required action writes to user storage, the account console writes locally, and the login authenticator then reads whichever the new getCredential helper finds first — under-scoped relative to the stated intent of 'recovery key support for user storage providers'.

[BUG] The recovery-code design has no mechanism to consume/invalidate a used code when the credential is managed by userStorage, so recovery codes remain permanently reusable. Recovery authn codes are a single-use control: the local-storage provider marks a used code as used after successful validation, but for a userStorage-backed credential there is no contract or hook (the test provider's isValid at BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage simply anyMatch-es the raw code list and never mutates it) — a user whose codes live in userStorage (or an attacker who saw one code) can reuse the same code indefinitely, defeating the purpose of recovery codes.

[ADVISORY] The provider id is hardcoded as the magic string "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" while the diff simultaneously removes the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID import and its constant usage in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction, leaving two spellings of the same discriminator. If the constant's value ever changes (or is typo'd in one of the copies), CredentialHelper.getProvider(...) returns null and createRecoveryCodesCredential throws an NPE on the local-storage fallback path; the previous code in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction used the constant precisely to prevent this drift.

[ADVISORY] The refactor wraps the lookup in Optional via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential but immediately calls Optional.get() with no isPresent() check, so the bean still crashes with NoSuchElementException when no credential exists. A userStorage user whose recovery-code credential was deleted or failed to deserialize (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns empty when neither federated nor local credentials match) who hits the recovery-code form gets a 500 instead of a challenge; the diff touched exactly this line and made the guard trivial but skipped it.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials deserialization failure is swallowed with a log line and the credential silently omitted from the returned stream, so a corrupt recovery-code payload makes the user appear to have no recovery codes. The test provider then reports isConfiguredFor=false and login falls through to the next alternative with no signal, so the stand-in test can pass (credential absent → skip) while the same corruption in a real federated store would silently lock users out of the recovery path.

[BUG] The raw (unhashed) generated codes are serialized into the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential, so the federated path persists plaintext recovery codes while the local fallback stores the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel — two different data shapes for the same credential type depending on storage location. Any userStorage provider adopting this contract ends up storing the full recovery-code list in cleartext (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage puts input's payload straight into credentialData), and a provider that assumed the same hashed model shape the local provider writes will misparse the credential; consumers reading credentials back (getCredentials/isValid) must implement a second, divergent deserialization path.

[BUG] The new Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() is immediately dereferenced with .get() instead of being checked for presence. When a user with no recovery-authn-codes credential (neither federated nor local) hits the login bean path (e.g. the authenticator is REQUIRED while the user never completed the required action), the constructor throws NoSuchElementException, producing a 500 error page instead of the graceful failure path the surrounding recovery flow promises; the switch to Optional also silently dropped the original code's assumption that only local storage was consulted, without adding any handling for the now-wider not-found case.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential ships the plaintext generated recovery codes to user storage via new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson), changing the credential contract from hashed, single-use codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel) to a raw JSON list. Any user storage that accepts the update stores recovery codes in plaintext and validates by plain string comparison (as the bundled BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does), so recovery codes for federated users lose both the hashing guarantee and the single-use guarantee that local-storage recovery codes retain — a silent weakening of the security intent with no flag or documentation that the semantics differ between the two storages.

[BUG] For the user-storage path the raw codes are serialized with JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString and wrapped in RuntimeException on IOException, aborting credential creation after the codes have already been displayed to the user. If JsonSerialization throws, the user has just been shown recovery codes on the required-action page but no credential is persisted, and the RuntimeException surfaces as a server error; additionally, the local-storage fallback branch (recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) is only reached when updateCredential returns false, so a user storage that accepts the type but fails mid-write leaves no local credential either.

[ADVISORY] The federated isValid() for recovery codes never consumes or invalidates a used code, diverging from the single-use semantics that the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider enforces. A user with a federated recovery-codes credential can replay the same recovery code indefinitely in the browser flow, defeating the one-time-use intent of recovery codes; the test added in this diff even exercises login but never asserts a second use fails, so the regression is invisible to the suite.

[ADVISORY] getCredential() returns the raw CredentialModel from federated storage without any validation that the model can be parsed by RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel, and prioritizes federated over local credentials unconditionally. If both a federated and a local recovery-codes credential exist (e.g. a user migrated off storage, or the fallback branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential ran earlier), the stale federated credential shadows the local one during login, so users are validated against codes they no longer possess; callers in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then parse a model whose shape depends on the arbitrary JSON the user storage wrote.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential passes the raw, plaintext recovery codes (JSON-serialized List<String>) to the federated user storage via UserCredentialModel.setChallengeResponse, while the local-storage branch stores only the SHA-256-hashed codes, so any user storage adopting this pattern persists usable one-time credential material in cleartext. A user storage provider implementing updateCredential for recovery codes (as the bundled BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage example in this diff does at line 189, storing input.getChallengeResponse() verbatim) ends up with all recovery codes recoverable in plaintext by anyone with read access to that store — a database dump or backup leak yields working authentication codes, unlike the Keycloak DB where only hashes are stored.

[BUG] When the recovery-code credential lives in user storage (the new path enabled by this diff via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential checking federated credentials first), the authenticator never updates the credential to consume the used code, so recovery codes are infinitely replayable. In the local-storage path, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider marks the used code/advances the index on successful authentication; in the federated path added here, BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid matches any code in the JSON list with no state change, so an attacker who observes or previously used one recovery code can replay it indefinitely — defeating the one-time-code design that limits the blast radius of a leaked code.

[ADVISORY] getCredential returns the federated credential in preference to the local one whenever both exist, so a user-storage-provided credential silently shadows a hash-protected Keycloak-stored credential. An operator migrating users from a storage provider that supports recovery codes gets the storage's plaintext, non-consuming validation semantics instead of the hashed local credential without any signal; combined with the replay gap above, users whose credentials exist in both places lose the local storage's consumed-code tracking.

[ADVISORY] The boolean result of updateCredential is the only signal distinguishing user-storage from local storage, and on a provider that returns true while silently not persisting (or persisting malformed data), the local credential creation is skipped with no error. A misbehaving or partially-implemented user storage causes recovery codes to be generated and shown to the user in the UI but never actually stored, so the user believes they have working recovery codes and cannot authenticate with them; no error surfaces to the user or admin.

[ADVISORY] The Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential is unwrapped with .get() without isPresent() check, replacing the previous getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get() with a broader two-source lookup that still throws NoSuchElementException when neither source has the credential. Any code path constructing this bean for a user without a recovery-code credential (e.g., a stale authentication session after an admin deletes the credential, or a storage returning an empty stream on transient error) crashes with an unhandled NoSuchElementException, producing a 500 page during login instead of a recoverable auth error.

[ADVISORY] The refactor to Optional adds no behavior and no test covers the empty-Optional path: the code still calls credentialModelOpt.get() unguarded, so the Optional wrapping is cosmetic and the NoSuchElementException crash path (user with no recovery-code credential reaching this bean) is exercised by no test in the diff. A maintainer reading 'Optional' assumes safe absence handling; the next change (or any flow configuration letting a user without a recovery-code credential hit this bean) throws NoSuchElementException with no test pinning the current throw-on-absent behavior either way.

[ADVISORY] The setupRecoveryKeysForUserWithRequiredAction helper's logoutOtherSessions parameter is only ever called with true, so the uncheckLogoutSessions branch (when false) added in this diff is dead test code that has never executed. The helper advertises a capability (testing the 'don't log out other sessions' path of RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction) that is never exercised, and a future caller passing false would run an untested branch for the first time in CI.

[ADVISORY] The new federated-storage recovery-code validation branch in isValid() is only tested through the happy path; the two failure returns added in this diff (stored credential null returns false at line ~330, and undecodable credentialData returns false at ~337) have no test that triggers them. A regression in the null-credential or deserialization-failure guards (e.g. someone reorders the null check or flips the return) passes the new testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin test because it only submits a valid code, so users of federated storage get silently accepted or wrongly rejected credentials without any test failing.

[ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin verifies only the first successful login with code index 0 and never asserts single-use consumption — no assertion that code 0 is burned, that a replay of the same code fails, or that a subsequent login requests code 1. If the federated-storage path loses code-consumption bookkeeping (the BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid() implementation has no consumed-code tracking at all — any of the generated codes validates on every attempt), this test still passes, giving false confidence that federated recovery codes behave like the built-in provider where used codes must not be reusable.

[ADVISORY] The local-storage fallback arm of getCredential() — the .or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)) branch that fires when the user has no federated credential — is exercised by no test in this diff, since testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only creates the credential in user storage. The fallback branch that recovers existing behavior for pure-Keycloak-DB users (the pre-change code path in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator and the login bean) is now covered only implicitly by tests outside this diff; a regression in the .or() ordering (e.g. swapping federated/local precedence) would not be caught by any test added for this feature.

[ADVISORY] The IOException catch in the new getCredentials() implementation swallows the error and silently omits the recovery-codes credential from the returned stream, and no test exercises this failure branch, so callers see an absent credential instead of an error. If stored credentialData is ever unparseable, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() finds nothing federated and falls through to the local-storage arm, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean throws NoSuchElementException on .get() — a chain of silent degradation with no test pinning or surfacing it.

[BUG] The federated write path stores the raw recovery codes as a plain JSON list in CredentialModel.credentialData (via UserCredentialModel("", TYPE, recoveryCodesJson) → BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential line ~192 `recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())`), which is a different schema than the one RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel expects to read back (credentialData must be the recovery-codes structured JSON with hashed codes). RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean (line ~21 of this diff) and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator call RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which returns the federated credential first, then feed it to RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...).getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().getNumber(); parsing the raw-list credentialData throws (or yields garbage), so any user whose recovery codes live in user storage hits a 500/parse failure on the recovery-code login form instead of a code prompt.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the plaintext generated codes (recoveryCodesJson) in the user-storage credential with no consumption/update path, so the same code validates forever; BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid (lines ~326-340 of this diff) checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` against the full original list and nothing in the diff removes or marks a code as used after successful login. Recovery authn codes for user-storage users are infinitely reusable, defeating their one-time-use guarantee: an attacker who observes one code (shoulder-surf, log leak) can log in repeatedly; the single-use semantics that the local-storage provider enforces are silently lost on the federated path.

[ADVISORY] The write is split-brained with no cutover guard: if updateCredential() returns true the raw codes go to user storage while the fully-populated hashed credentialModel (which was already built by the caller, RecoveryAuthnCodesAction line ~116) is discarded, and if it returns false the raw codes never reach user storage — there is no dual-write or cleanup, so a user storage that partially persists (e.g. returns true before failing internally) leaves the credential present in federated state and absent locally, and getCredential's federated-first lookup then masks a local credential forever. Admins who later regenerate codes locally (or a storage that starts returning false after an outage) end up with two divergent credential sets, and RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential always prefers the (stale) federated one, so users authenticate against codes they were never shown and the newly generated set is silently unreachable.

[ADVISORY] The refactor replaced a previously guaranteed-present local-credential lookup with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) but still calls `.get()` on the Optional unguarded — and getCredential returns Optional.empty() when the user has neither a federated nor a local recovery credential, a state the old code could not reach on this bean's call path but the new federated-first path can (e.g. storage returns true from supportsCredentialType but the user never completed setup). Any render of the recovery-code login page for a federated user whose storage reports the credential type as supported but holds no credential for that user throws NoSuchElementException instead of falling back to another authenticator or showing a friendly error.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials() returns a recovery-code CredentialModel whose credentialData is the raw generated-code list (line ~192 write) rather than the hashed-codes structure every other consumer of getCredentialsStream assumes, so this test fixture encodes the schema drift as the reference behavior for future user-storage implementers. Third-party user-storage developers copying this fixture will persist plaintext single-use codes in credentialData (a non-secret field surfaced by admin/account REST credential listings), leaking recovery codes to anyone who can read credential metadata.

[BUG] The bean calls Optional.get() on RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without handling the empty case, and the new federated path makes empty reachable for users who are reported as configured. A user whose recovery codes live in a user storage that does not implement CredentialLookupProvider (so getFederatedCredentialsStream yields nothing) has isConfiguredFor()==true via CredentialInputValidator, reaches the recovery-code login form, and the bean throws NoSuchElementException — a raw 500 during login page render instead of a rendered challenge, for a credential the realm says exists.

[BUG] getCredentials() catches IOException from JsonSerialization.readValue and silently omits the recovery credential from the returned stream with only a log line. A corrupted/unparseable recoveryCodes payload makes the credential invisible to getCredential()/account console while isValid() still fails closed at login, so the user is told they have no recovery codes but is still prompted to enter one (or crashes the login bean via the Optional.get() in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean since the stream is now empty) — silent partial success with inconsistent state.

[ADVISORY] The user-storage path serializes the raw, plaintext recovery codes (recoveryCodesJson) and passes them as the credential payload via updateCredential, while the local path stores the hashed credentialModel — the same logical operation takes two materially different persist paths. Any user storage that persists the challengeResponse verbatim (as the reference provider in this diff does, storing the raw JSON in credentialData) holds usable recovery codes in cleartext; a read-only leak of that store's data is directly redeemable for account takeover, and the two divergent write shapes mean a storage migration of this field changes semantics mid-life.

[ADVISORY] The provider id is hardcoded as the string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, and the provider is fetched unconditionally before knowing which branch is taken. If the provider id string ever changes or the provider is absent (feature not registered), session.getProvider throws with a provider-lookup error at recovery-code setup time rather than a clear message naming the feature, and the removed import of the factory constant in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction leaves two parallel spellings of the same id to keep in sync — the next rename breaks one silently.

goldens.comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

adjudication.rationale: The new CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential() serializes the *raw* generated recovery codes list to JSON and passes it into a UserCredentialModel as the challengeResponse ("recoveryCodesJson"), then calls user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...). If the user storage accepts the credential (returns true), the only persisted data is this plaintext JSON list. This is directly reflected in the diff’s BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential(): for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE it stores input.getChallengeResponse() into credentialData verbatim. In contrast, the local-storage path calls recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel), where credentialModel is the structured RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel (expected to contain hashed/salted representation). Thus the diff introduces a security/correctness inconsistency where federated/user-storage persistence stores secrets in plaintext at rest.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The user-storage branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential provides no mechanism to mark an individual code as used, because the one-shot UserCredentialModel.updateCredential call only ever writes the full raw list on (re)generation. For user-storage users every recovery code remains valid forever (the storage provider's isValid in this diff compares the submitted code against the full original list with no consumed-code tracking), so a leaked code can be replayed indefinitely, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean always prompts for code number 0 since the rebuilt model from createFromValues never has any code marked used.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds recovery-codes support for federated/user-storage users by storing the generated codes as a JSON list (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential -> UserCredentialModel(..., recoveryCodesJson) -> user.credentialManager().updateCredential). In the shown user-storage implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage), the recovery-codes branch persists only the full list as credentialData and validates with `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` (no removal/consumption, no used-state tracking). Nothing in the diff updates the stored list on successful use, so recovery codes remain replayable indefinitely for user-storage users. Additionally, getCredentials reconstructs the model via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(<List>, ...)`, which (given only raw strings) cannot reflect any used codes, making the UI logic that asks for `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get().getNumber()` plausibly always return the first code index.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The recovery-codes credential provider is looked up via the hardcoded string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, which the removed code in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction previously used. The provider id is now maintained in two places (the factory constant and this literal); if the constant is ever changed or a deployer swaps the provider, the literal silently resolves to null and createCredential throws an NPE at recovery-code setup time for local-storage users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a hardcoded provider id lookup in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential`: `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")`, and it then unconditionally calls `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)` if `updateCredential` returns false. There is no null-check, so if that provider id ever doesn’t resolve, this would NPE. However, the finding’s core claim that this is *currently* inconsistent with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID` cannot be verified from the diff because the factory constant value is not shown; the issue is therefore a concrete maintainability/robustness concern grounded in the change, not a demonstrable present-day defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes registers a "delayed-authenticator" execution with a delay config (and a misspelled alias "delayed-suthenticator-config") even though every caller in this diff passes delay=0, making the delayed subflow dead weight that must resolve successfully for the test to run. If the "delayed-authenticator" provider id does not exist in the test auth-server's deployed providers, FlowUtil.addAuthenticatorExecution fails and testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin errors before reaching any assertion; even when it resolves, the next maintainer must edit this flow wiring to change any test's timing behavior.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes, the copied browser flow is wired to include a REQUIRED "delayed-authenticator" execution with config alias "delayed-suthenticator-config" and a "delay" parameter. adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the code uses `boolean userStorageCreated = user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential);` as the sole gate to decide whether to skip local creation (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`). There is no follow-up verification (e.g., read-back via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` / `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream()` as added in `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`) and no handling of a provider returning `true` while not actually persisting valid data. Any code path constructing this bean for a user without a recovery-code credential (e.g., a stale authentication session after an admin deletes the credential, or a storage returning an empty stream on transient error) crashes with an unhandled NoSuchElementException, producing a 500 page during login instead of a recoverable auth error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The local-storage fallback arm of getCredential() — the .or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)) branch that fires when the user has no federated credential — is exercised by no test in this diff, since testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only creates the credential in user storage. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The IOException catch in the new getCredentials() implementation swallows the error and silently omits the recovery-codes credential from the returned stream, and no test exercises this failure branch, so callers see an absent credential instead of an error. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The federated write path stores the raw recovery codes as a plain JSON list in CredentialModel.credentialData (via UserCredentialModel("", TYPE, recoveryCodesJson) → BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential line ~192 `recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())`), which is a different schema than the one RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel expects to read back (credentialData must be the recovery-codes structured JSON with hashed codes). adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the plaintext generated codes (recoveryCodesJson) in the user-storage credential with no consumption/update path, so the same code validates forever; BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid (lines ~326-340 of this diff) checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` against the full original list and nothing in the diff removes or marks a code as used after successful login. Recovery authn codes for user-storage users are infinitely reusable, defeating their one-time-use guarantee: an attacker who observes one code (shoulder-surf, log leak) can log in repeatedly; the single-use semantics that the local-storage provider enforces are silently lost on the federated path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a federated/user-storage path for recovery codes by serializing the full generated code list into `UserCredentialModel` (`createRecoveryCodesCredential(..., recoveryCodesJson)`) and persisting it via `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. In the user-storage implementation shown (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid`), validation for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` deserializes the stored list and returns `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`, with no code removal/marking-used/update on success anywhere in this diff. That makes any observed valid code reusable indefinitely for federated users, violating one-time-use semantics and creating a security defect introduced/exposed by these changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The write is split-brained with no cutover guard: if updateCredential() returns true the raw codes go to user storage while the fully-populated hashed credentialModel (which was already built by the caller, RecoveryAuthnCodesAction line ~116) is discarded, and if it returns false the raw codes never reach user storage — there is no dual-write or cleanup, so a user storage that partially persists (e.g. returns true before failing internally) leaves the credential present in federated state and absent locally, and getCredential's federated-first lookup then masks a local credential forever. Admins who later regenerate codes locally (or a storage that starts returning false after an outage) end up with two divergent credential sets, and RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential always prefers the (stale) federated one, so users authenticate against codes they were never shown and the newly generated set is silently unreachable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces split storage paths for recovery codes without any cutover/cleanup, and also changes reads to prefer federated credentials. In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, if `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` returns true, only the raw JSON codes are written to user storage and no local credential is created; if it returns false, the local provider is used (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`) but there is no removal of any existing federated recovery-codes credential. Separately, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` explicitly searches federated credentials first and only falls back to local. Therefore, if a federated recovery-codes credential exists and later a new local one is created (e.g., updateCredential returns false due to a provider change/outage), the stale federated credential will mask the newly-generated local credential indefinitely, causing authentication to be checked against the wrong set of codes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The refactor replaced a previously guaranteed-present local-credential lookup with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) but still calls `.get()` on the Optional unguarded — and getCredential returns Optional.empty() when the user has neither a federated nor a local recovery credential, a state the old code could not reach on this bean's call path but the new federated-first path can (e.g. storage returns true from supportsCredentialType but the user never completed setup). Any render of the recovery-code login page for a federated user whose storage reports the credential type as supported but holds no credential for that user throws NoSuchElementException instead of falling back to another authenticator or showing a friendly error.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the diff changes the lookup to `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and then immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence. The new helper `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` can return `Optional.empty()` when neither a federated nor stored recovery-codes credential exists, which would trigger a `NoSuchElementException` during page rendering.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredentials() returns a recovery-code CredentialModel whose credentialData is the raw generated-code list (line ~192 write) rather than the hashed-codes structure every other consumer of getCredentialsStream assumes, so this test fixture encodes the schema drift as the reference behavior for future user-storage implementers. Third-party user-storage developers copying this fixture will persist plaintext single-use codes in credentialData (a non-secret field surfaced by admin/account REST credential listings), leaking recovery codes to anyone who can read credential metadata.

adjudication.rationale: In the testsuite fixture `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage`, the new recovery-codes handling stores the generated codes JSON directly into `CredentialModel.credentialData` (`updateCredential`: `recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse());`), and `getCredentials()` later deserializes that same `credentialData` back into a `List` (`JsonSerialization.readValue(myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData(), List.class)`) to build a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The user-storage path serializes the raw, plaintext recovery codes (recoveryCodesJson) and passes them as the credential payload via updateCredential, while the local path stores the hashed credentialModel — the same logical operation takes two materially different persist paths. Any user storage that persists the challengeResponse verbatim (as the reference provider in this diff does, storing the raw JSON in credentialData) holds usable recovery codes in cleartext; a read-only leak of that store's data is directly redeemable for account takeover, and the two divergent write shapes mean a storage migration of this field changes semantics mid-life.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` which, on the user-storage/federated path, serializes `generatedCodes` to JSON (`recoveryCodesJson`) and passes it as the `UserCredentialModel` challenge/secret (`new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)`), then calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. Meanwhile the local-storage path calls `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`, which stores the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` rather than the raw JSON payload, creating materially different persistence semantics and a cleartext secret exposure in the user-storage path.
